1:
The first word of the chapter is plural in Hebrew, and that divides the group sharply. Gill takes the plural at face value and finds three persons in it, assigning creation to the Father as God of all flesh, to the Son by whom all things were made, and to the Spirit who moved on the waters. Henry does the same, pointing to the parallel plural in the question, Where is God my Makers, and to the deliberation before man was made. Ellicott notes only that the noun stands plural like the divine name itself, and lists other places where Maker is plural. Clarke will have none of it, and his objection is textual: the word is singular in a hundred and seventy-six of Kennicott's manuscripts and ninety-six of De Rossi's, in many old editions and in all the ancient versions, so the support this verse offers the doctrine is precarious. He then generalizes: men who load doubtful texts with weight do the truth no service, and whatever their intentions are its worst friends, their help being assistance to its adversaries.

On the duty itself they are of one mind and differ only in framing. Henry reads it twice over, as the preacher's application of all he has said about vanity and as the physician's antidote to the diseases of youth, the love of mirth and indulgence of the senses. Remembering, he insists, is not acknowledging that God made us but paying him what that fact obliges; and the days of youth are the days of choice, in which a man begins as he means to continue. Wesley presses the timing three ways — youth is when a man is most able, when the act is most acceptable, and when it best provides against old age and death — and calls it the surest evidence of sincerity. Clarke turns it into a claim of ownership: you are not your own and have no right to yourselves, since the one who made you also feeds and upholds you, and made you for a happiness found nowhere else. Gill supplies the plainest reason: young men are apt to forget there is a God at all.

The evil days are described rather than named, beginning with a darkening sky. Wesley observes that the added phrase about light shows the darkening is not of the luminaries but of the light they give men, and offers two readings: the face, whose complexion and lively eyes fade, or external circumstances, where the joy of youth turns to sorrow. Gill reports the same two from older Jewish authorities, adds a third taking it literally of failing eyesight, and rejects that because dim sight is described later in its own right; he prefers the faculties of the soul, understanding and judgment and will. Clarke reverses direction and reads the first half of the verse of the prime of life, the returning clouds being the winter of old age. Delitzsch takes the days of evil as feeble, helpless age, and rejects the reading that makes the whole a storm gathering before death.

Ellicott declines to compete. The style rises here, he says, and as often with highly wrought poetry the general effect is easier to perceive than the words producing it. English readers have been deeply impressed by the verses about the silver cord and the golden bowl, and in his judgment gain very little from commentators' efforts to tell them what those figures mean. Having used all the help his predecessors could give, he owns frankly that he can offer no more than a vague account of the imagery here. On the clouds he ventures only that darkness in the heavens is a standing symbol of calamity, while Wesley takes the endless succession of rain and cloud for either the rheums that flow incessantly in old men or the unbroken sequence of infirmities, one deep calling to another.
3:
The house is the body, and most fittings are agreed. Clarke numbers them: the keepers are the hands, growing palsied; the strong men the legs, no longer able to carry the weight; the grinders the teeth, so decayed that soft food becomes the only food; those who look out of the windows the optic nerves, whose humours thicken until images no longer come clearly. Gill canvasses alternatives: the Targum made the keepers the knees, older authorities the ribs, which he rejects since ribs are fixed to the backbone and cannot tremble; he follows Aben Ezra to the hands and arms, which feed and defend the body and in age grow stiff. On the doors of the next verse he prefers the lips: an old man neither cares to speak, his voice having failed, nor opens his mouth to eat, and while eating keeps it shut, no teeth being left to hold the food in.

Two of them resist the anatomy. Ellicott begins from the picture, seeing a household in consternation — servants below, masters in equal distress, grinding maids stopping work, ladies driven back from the lattices. He grants that the house means the bodily frame, but warns that the English grinders suggests teeth in a way the Hebrew grinding maidens does not, and that when an anatomical equivalent is found for every image the reading becomes so forced that some prefer to treat the verse as general alarm at a storm. Delitzsch records a similar line, continuing the night of the previous verse: watchers guarding the house, labourers worn out, maids gone to rest, the women at the windows unrecognisable in the dark. He reports without embarrassment the old Jewish reading of the doors as the body's apertures, citing the morning benediction that blesses God for forming man with cavities.

At the bird everyone falters. Ellicott sets out three explanations — the old man wakes at a chirp, his own voice thins to a chirp, or a bird of ill omen cries — says each meets serious objections, and declines to argue, having nothing better to offer. Wesley takes the first, the old man weary of lying and rising as the birds begin. The almond divides them further. Wesley and Clarke both read a head as white as the tree in flower, Clarke adding a traveller's report of the almond in bloom in Judea looking like an old man with white locks; but Clarke insists the verb means not to flourish but to fall off, so the hair, an animal vegetable without nourishment, whitens and drops. Ellicott renders the same verb as causing loathing, and continues in that key: the locust, ordinarily a favourite eastern food, becomes a burden, and the caper berry, which the English renders desire, fails.

The last figures get precise organs from two of them and none from the rest. Clarke identifies the silver cord as the spinal marrow, named for its shape, colour and preciousness, and the golden bowl as the brain within the skull, adding that the final loosening is the falling of the lower jaw, the one infallible sign of death. Wesley agrees and adds the membranes of the brain, drawn out to a great fineness; Gill mentions only an older reading making the cord the string of the tongue. Delitzsch describes the architecture instead: three successive clauses, the first showing the old man in general discomfort, the second the weaknesses that forerun death, the third the dissolution. On the returning spirit he is careful. The verse gives no comfort of itself, and the notion of a personal spirit going to God with consciousness intact is foreign to it; yet what the book earlier raised as an open question, whether man's spirit rises where a beast's descends, is here stated as fact. Ellicott says as much in a line, and Clarke concludes that the author of the book was no materialist.
8:
The motto returns and everyone treats it as deliberate. Gill points out that the proposition stated at the opening has been proved by an induction of particulars and is repeated as a settled result, all things under the sun being vanity in the superlative. Henry has the preacher unwilling to part with his hearers until he carries his point, and offers the formula that what we see daily proved should be daily improved. Clarke lets dissolution supply the force: now that man, the masterpiece of creation, is dust, what remains that is stable? Wesley marks the repetition as the argument's due conclusion.

What follows raises the question who is speaking. Ellicott holds the epilogue an integral part of the book, its author, having until now reported the preacher's words, here speaking in his own person to tell readers that the man whose teaching he preserves was also a writer. Delitzsch takes a similar view, describing an author who had introduced Koheleth as speaker and now continues on his own account; the connecting conjunction, he insists, is only an external join, and nothing is more unwarranted than making the motto itself the postscript's opening on that ground. He also rejects a rendering by which it remains to be added that Koheleth was wise, since after a whole book of his wisdom nothing of the sort remains. Gill, Clarke and Wesley pass over the question and read the verses as the preacher recommending his own writings, Wesley noting that he weighed matter and words rather than uttering whatever came to mind. Henry builds the credentials instead: these are the words of a penitent gathered home from his wanderings, of a man wiser than his neighbours, of one who used his wisdom to do good — and preachers, he adds, need wisdom to win souls.

On the acceptable words all guard against one misunderstanding. Gill insists the phrase means doctrines rather than elegant style, while allowing that a preacher should look for language fit to convey right ideas. Clarke says the words were the best and most suitable, those the people could understand, and adds the limit: not words that merely please them, but words of truth. Delitzsch makes the double aim explicit, the preacher seeking at once a pleasing form and exact truth, and rejects a construction turning the second clause into a separate infinitive. Wesley wants them to comfort and profit.

The goads and nails prove harder. Delitzsch establishes the goad from the Greek versions and a rabbinic list of driving-rods, spending the rest of his note on pointing. Gill takes the goad as it stands, sharp sticks for driving cattle, applied to doctrine that pierces a sinner's heart. The second image divides them. Wesley makes the masters of assemblies the teachers of the church, and the one shepherd Christ. Clarke reports a theory that they were officers appointed by the prince to keep anything unprofitable from the people's hands, a scribe taking down a wise man's words and a master checking them — something like a licenser of the press, he says, before admitting that such officials are little more than conjecture, and that the phrase may simply mean public teachers. Ellicott doubts everything here. The words are enigmatical, he says, and their precise sense uncertain; the English represents the original fairly once the reader notices that two key words are supplied; and since the term rendered assemblies might as easily mean collections of sayings as gatherings of people, he makes nothing of the closing clause beyond this, that the sages were given to instruct the people by Israel's Shepherd. His contrast for the next verse is the sharpest thing here: the weighty sayings of the wise against the volubility of modern bookmakers. Clarke, writing two thousand years after the warning, observes that millions of treatises have since been added, the press still groans, and no subject is exhausted.
13:
The last two verses are read as the answer the book has worked toward. Henry states the question — what is that good which men should do, and what the certain way to their great end — and says the search failed everywhere until it arrived here, at the old discovery that serious godliness is the only road to happiness. He makes a point of the pronoun: the preacher says not Do you hear it but Let us hear it, since a man who teaches others and not himself is a teacher by halves; and he notes that the Hebrew scribes marked the verse as weighty with an enlarged letter. Gill hears a closing formula, the book ending with everything worth regard compressed into a few words. Delitzsch treats the phrase as a heading rather than an exhortation, the final result once everything has been learned, and rejects the rendering that turns the opening into an invitation for us all to listen, since the pronoun would then be used of persons where this author almost always uses it of things.

The prescription needs no interpreting, and they spend their space on its reach. Henry locates the root of religion in a fear reigning in the heart, made of reverence for God's majesty, deference to his authority and dread of his anger. Wesley takes the word for the whole inward worship of God, reverence and love and trust and a heart given to pleasing him. Clarke reduces the commandments to the two on which they hang, and observes with satisfaction that neither much reading nor much study is needed to obey them — a remark that draws its force from the warning about books a verse earlier, and from his own note that millions of volumes have been written on this one sentence.

The clause that follows is where they divide, and the dispute is about a word that is not in the Hebrew. Clarke objects that the noun duty, supplied by the English translators, spoils the sense and perhaps perverts it: the Hebrew says the whole of Adam, all that God required of the first man and his posterity, though he grants the gospel must be brought in to fill out so short a saying. Ellicott corrects the English differently, rendering the duty of every man rather than the whole duty of man, and finds there an anticipation of the apostle's argument that God is not the God of one nation only. Delitzsch reaches the same place from grammar, the clause expressing an obligation lying on every man without exception. Wesley keeps the traditional sense and expands it: this is a man's whole work, his whole perfection, and the sum of all he needs to know or do or enjoy.

The judgment that closes the book is taken by all to be a real one, and by one of them to settle the book's whole argument. Ellicott makes the case. Since the work is filled with complaints about the imperfection of retribution in this life, an announcement that every work and every secret thing will be brought into judgment can mean nothing but a judgment after death; so a book of sceptical debate ends by stating, more plainly than anywhere else in the Old Testament, that God will judge the secrets of men. Gill agrees in a line, referring it to the great judgment as the Targum does. Delitzsch presses the concealment: the judgment is one from whose cognition nothing hidden escapes. Clarke sets out the reasoning in numbered steps and adds what the others omit, that the good godly men tried to conceal will be brought to light as surely as the evil the wicked hid; and he closes on a sentence answering the motto, that although here all is vanity, there vanities will be vain no more. Wesley makes the same point of thoughts against actions.
